Animation · Culture

Japan put 229 student animations inside one museum.

ICAF 2026 closes in Tokyo today. Its scale—34 schools, four screening days and hundreds of works—shows an animation culture much wider than the commercial series exported around the world.

By Yuji Shimizu · YUJI @ Japan
Published October 12, 2026 · 12:10 JST · 5 min read

On the third floor of the National Art Center, Tokyo, a different map of Japanese animation is reaching its final frame today. It does not begin with a television network, a famous manga or a merchandise campaign. It begins with classrooms.

The Inter College Animation Festival—ICAF—has assembled 229 student works from 34 universities, art colleges and specialist schools. Screenings began October 9 and conclude October 12 with school programs, special selections and a closing ceremony. Admission is free, and the venue is the museum’s auditorium and training room in Roppongi.

The number matters because “Japanese animation” is often reduced overseas to the commercial anime pipeline. ICAF is a view of what exists before that pipeline narrows choices into broadcast lengths, franchise designs and production schedules. Student films can be minute-long experiments, drawn narratives, stop-motion pieces, abstract motion or difficult personal work. They do not have to look like the anime already on a streaming homepage.

The festival’s real subject is not 229 possible TV directors. It is 229 answers to a more open question: what can a moving image made in Japan become?

Thirty-four schools, not one “anime style”

The participating institutions stretch across Japan and approach animation through different traditions. Art universities may place drawing, sculpture and experimental film beside animation. Technology schools can bring digital production and interactive thinking. Specialist programs often emphasize craft and employability. Putting their selections together makes the differences visible.

That comparison is central to ICAF’s design. Programs are organized by participating school, so viewers can notice how teaching environments shape rhythm, sound, technique and subject matter. The festival also maintains a database of works and publishes digest material, allowing audiences to move beyond a single prize-winning title.

ICAF describes itself as the “front line of student animation.” The phrase is useful if “front line” means a place where methods are still unstable. Commercial Japanese animation depends on enormous skill, but production risk is expensive. A student film can make an awkward, beautiful or unresolved choice precisely because it has not yet become a product.

Why a national museum matters

The National Art Center is unusual among Japanese museums because it does not hold a permanent collection of its own. Instead, its large Roppongi building hosts changing exhibitions and art-association shows. Placing student animation there frames the work as contemporary art and education, not merely as recruitment material for studios.

There is a second signal in the price: free admission. A curious visitor can encounter work from schools they may never visit, while students can watch peers from across the country on a cinema-scale screen. The exchange is professional development, but it is also public culture.

This year’s four-day schedule ends on Sports Day, a national holiday. That coincidence gives the final day a larger potential audience and an interesting contrast. Japan’s best-known animation circulates globally through expensive franchises; here, future creators share a museum room before their names are familiar.

How to watch without treating it as an audition

It is tempting to ask which student will become famous. That is the least interesting first question. Look instead for decisions: Does the film move on every frame or leave stillness? Is sound carrying the story? Does the director build a world, document a memory, or turn texture itself into the subject? A rough film can contain one idea that a polished film would avoid.

The official database identifies titles and schools, and the festival’s “ICAF Picks” and special programs provide a curated route through the larger field. With 229 works, nobody needs to pretend to see everything. The scale is the point: there is no single conveyor belt carrying students toward one Japanese visual language.

Today’s Japanese word connects directly to the event: 上映 (jōei), meaning a public screening or showing of a film. 上 means “up” or “to raise,” and 映 means “to project” or “reflect.” You will see jōei on cinema and festival schedules: jōei wa nanji kara desu ka?—“What time does the screening begin?” It is more specific than simply watching a video; it points to the organized act of putting a work before an audience.

ICAF 2026’s physical festival ends today, while its official site remains available through October 25. That gives overseas readers a route into the database and digest material even if they cannot reach Roppongi. The important discovery is already visible in the count: Japan’s animation future is being drawn in dozens of schools at once.
